title: Multilingual Tokenization & Cost
scopeHtml: Scope: How language and script change token counts, latency and cost, and how to budget for it.

notes.title: Why the same sentence costs different amounts
notes.html:
Plain words. An LLM does not read letters or words. It reads tokens: chunks of text from a fixed list (the vocabulary) that was built before the model was trained. You are billed per token, the context window is measured in tokens, and generation speed is tokens per second. So the question "how much does this cost?" is really "how many tokens is this text?", and that number depends on the language and script of the text, not just on its meaning.

The core fact. Two sentences that mean exactly the same thing can differ by 2x to 10x in token count. A tokenizer built mostly from English web text has long, efficient tokens for English ("the", " and", "ing") and only short fragments, sometimes single bytes, for languages and scripts it saw less often.

Why it exists. Tokenizers are trained by a compression-style algorithm (see tokenization notes: BPE merges the most frequent adjacent pairs). Whatever is frequent in the training sample gets long tokens. If 50 percent of the sample is English and 0.1 percent is Amharic, English wins the merge budget. Nobody planned it as a price list; it is a side effect of data mix plus a fixed vocabulary size.

What it changes, in four places.

more tokens for the same meaning
   |
   +--> input cost   (billed per input token)
   +--> output cost  (billed per output token, usually 3-5x input price)
   +--> latency      (each output token is one sequential decode step)
   +--> context      (the window holds fewer words of that language)

Illustrative numbers (rough, tokenizer-dependent, verify with your model). On older OpenAI-style tokenizers, a typical English sentence is about 1.3 tokens per word. Spanish, French and German are often 1.5 to 2x English. Russian, Arabic, Hebrew and Greek are often 2 to 3x. Hindi, Tamil, Thai, Burmese and Amharic can be 4 to 10x. Chinese and Japanese depend heavily on the tokenizer: older ones spend about 1 to 2 tokens per character, newer large-vocabulary ones spend closer to 1 token per character or even less for common words. Treat all of these as ranges to measure, not constants.

See also: the tokenization notes (02_K1) give the basic rule of thumb (4 characters per token in English) and one paragraph on inflation. This note goes deeper: the mechanism in bytes, how to measure fertility, the cost and latency arithmetic, code, and budgeting.

Real life. Think of a postal service that charges per box, and boxes come in sizes tuned to English-shaped parcels. A parcel shaped differently has to be split across several boxes, and you pay for each box even though the contents are the same.

Tech. Token count is a compression ratio. A tokenizer that compresses English at 4.5 characters per token and Hindi at 1.2 characters per token is giving Hindi users a worse compression ratio, and cost, latency and context all scale with that ratio.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "cost depends on words" or "characters". It depends on tokens, and the words-to-tokens ratio differs per language and per model.
  • Assuming the 4-characters-per-token rule works for non-English text. It is an English average only.
  • Believing that two models with the same price per million tokens cost the same. Different tokenizers produce different counts for identical text.

notes.title: Token fertility: the metric to know
notes.html:
What it is. Fertility is tokens per word (or per "unit of meaning") for a given tokenizer and language. Lower is better. Since "word" is hard to define in Chinese, Japanese and Thai (no spaces), people also use tokens per character, or compare against a parallel text (the same document professionally translated) and use the ratio versus English.

The parity ratio. Take a parallel corpus, such as FLORES-200, which has the same sentences in about 200 languages (verify the exact language count in its docs). Tokenize each language and compute:

premium(lang) = tokens(lang text) / tokens(English text)

Example (made-up round numbers for the math):
  English sentence: 20 tokens
  Hindi sentence:   70 tokens   -> premium = 70 / 20 = 3.5x
  Spanish sentence: 28 tokens   -> premium = 28 / 20 = 1.4x

A premium of 3.5x means: 3.5x the input bill, 3.5x the output bill, 3.5x the decode time for that sentence, and the context window fits 1/3.5 as much of that language.

Research behind it. Studies of "tokenization parity" and "language model tokenizers introduce unfairness between languages" (Petrov et al., 2023, NeurIPS; verify the exact title) measured premiums of up to several times, and in extreme cases an order of magnitude, between English and other languages on popular tokenizers. The same work argued that API pricing per token therefore charges speakers of some languages more for the same service. Fast-moving: newer tokenizers have narrowed the gap, so always re-measure.

Where fertility comes from, step by step.

  1. The tokenizer is trained on a sample of text. The language mix of the sample decides which merges are learned first.
  2. Merges are learned in order of frequency until the vocabulary is full (for example 100k, 128k, 200k or 256k entries).
  3. English words and common code patterns get early merges, so they end up as one token.
  4. A language with 100x less data may never reach the merge budget; its words stay as syllable-sized or character-sized pieces, or fall all the way back to bytes.
  5. At inference time the tokenizer applies the merges greedily; fertility is the measured outcome.

Real products. OpenAI's cl100k_base (GPT-3.5/4 era) has about 100k tokens; o200k_base (GPT-4o and later) doubled the vocabulary to about 200k, and OpenAI stated that it improved compression for many non-English languages (verify the quoted ratios in the release notes). Meta's Llama 3 moved from a 32k SentencePiece vocabulary (Llama 2) to a 128k tiktoken-style vocabulary, partly for better multilingual compression. Google's Gemma uses a 256k SentencePiece vocabulary built for multilingual text. Multilingual models such as BLOOM and mT5 deliberately balanced their tokenizer training data.

Real life. Fertility is like exchange rates: one unit of meaning is worth a different number of "coins" (tokens) depending on the currency (language). The rate is set by who used the mint (the training data) the most.

Tech. It is the same quantity as compression ratio in information theory; comparing across languages needs a fair "unit of content", which is why parallel corpora are used instead of raw word counts.

Common interview traps.

  • Comparing tokens per word across languages that define "word" differently (Chinese, Thai, German compounds). Use a parallel corpus or tokens per character instead.
  • Using a single number for "non-English". Fertility ranges from near-English (Spanish) to extreme (Burmese); it is per language and per script.
  • Treating the bigger vocabulary as a guaranteed fix. It helps the languages that were added to training, not automatically all of them.

notes.title: Bytes, UTF-8 and why scripts differ
notes.html:
What a byte-level tokenizer sees. Modern LLM tokenizers are mostly byte-level BPE: the text is first converted to UTF-8 bytes, and merges are learned over bytes. This guarantees no unknown input, but it means the number of starting symbols for a character is its UTF-8 byte length.

UTF-8 byte lengths.

Script / characters Bytes per character
ASCII letters, digits, basic punctuation 1
Latin with accents (e, u with marks), Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic 2
Devanagari, Tamil, Thai, Bengali, most CJK 3
Emoji and rare historic scripts 4

Worked example (the math). The Hindi word "namaste" is written with six Unicode code points: न, म, स, ्, त, े. Each is in the Devanagari block, so each is 3 bytes in UTF-8.

6 code points x 3 bytes = 18 bytes
English "Hello" = 5 characters x 1 byte = 5 bytes

If the tokenizer has no merges for these Devanagari byte sequences, the
worst case is 1 token per byte = 18 tokens, versus 1 token for " Hello".
Real tokenizers have some merges, so the real count is lower (often 4 to 8
here) but still several times English.

Why combining marks matter. In Indic scripts a visible "letter" can be a base consonant plus a vowel sign plus a virama (the ् mark that joins consonants). A single user-visible syllable can be 2 to 4 code points, which is 6 to 12 bytes. Humans see one glyph; the tokenizer sees a byte string it may never have merged.

Byte fallback. SentencePiece-based tokenizers (Llama 2, Gemma, T5 family) can use byte fallback: if a character is not in the vocabulary, it is emitted as its raw bytes, written like <0xE0> <0xA4> <0xA8>. These byte tokens each count as one token. A rare character costs up to 3 or 4 tokens. This is why unusual scripts and emoji sequences look expensive.

Chinese, Japanese, Korean. Characters are 3 bytes but carry a lot of meaning each (a Chinese character is closer to a syllable-word than a Latin letter). Large vocabularies include thousands of common Han characters and many multi-character words as single tokens. So the same message is often shorter in tokens than in English-looking bytes, but less common characters (rare names, traditional variants) still fall back to 2 to 3 byte tokens.

Right-to-left and mixed text. Arabic and Hebrew are 2 bytes per letter. Arabic also has diacritics (tashkeel) and the tatweel stretching character; text with full diacritics (for example Quranic text) can cost more tokens than plain text.

Emoji and ZWJ sequences. A family emoji is several emoji joined by zero-width joiners (U+200D); one visible symbol can be 7+ code points and 20+ bytes, often 10+ tokens.

Real products. tiktoken (OpenAI) is the reference byte-level BPE implementation; you can run enc.encode("नमस्ते") and see the tokens. Hugging Face tokenizers and sentencepiece expose byte-fallback options. Gemini and Claude tokenizers differ and are not public in the same way; use each provider's token counting endpoint (below).

Real life. UTF-8 is a shipping manifest where English letters are small envelopes (1 unit), and Devanagari or Thai letters are bigger packages (3 units). If the tokenizer has no special pallets for those packages, every package ships alone.

Tech. Token count is bounded between "characters x merge efficiency" and "bytes". For a script with no merges, tokens approach UTF-8 byte count; with good merges, tokens approach word count.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "characters" when the right unit is bytes (or code points). len("नमस्ते") is 6 in Python but len("नमस्ते".encode("utf-8")) is 18.
  • Forgetting normalization: the same visible text can be NFC or NFD (accent as one code point or two). Different byte forms tokenize differently. Normalize text before counting or caching by hash.
  • Thinking emoji are cheap. ZWJ sequences and skin-tone modifiers multiply tokens.

notes.title: Measuring token counts in code
notes.html:
The rule. Never estimate multilingual cost by hand. Count with the model's own tokenizer, per language, on your real data. Below, the same idea in three languages: count tokens and compute the premium against English.

Python with tiktoken (OpenAI tokenizers; works as a stand-in estimate for other models, not exact).

# pip install tiktoken
import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")  # also "cl100k_base"; verify names in the tiktoken repo

samples = {
    "en": "Where is the nearest train station?",
    "hi": "निकटतम रेलवे स्टेशन कहाँ है?",
    "ja": "最寄りの駅はどこですか？",
    "ar": "أين أقرب محطة قطار؟",
}

base = len(enc.encode(samples["en"]))
for lang, text in samples.items():
    n = len(enc.encode(text))
    b = len(text.encode("utf-8"))
    # prints: language, code points, UTF-8 bytes, tokens, premium vs English
    print(f"{lang}: chars={len(text)} bytes={b} tokens={n} premium={n / base:.2f}x")

Kotlin with jtokkit (a JVM port of tiktoken, com.knuddels:jtokkit).

// build.gradle.kts: implementation("com.knuddels:jtokkit:<version>")  // verify latest version
import com.knuddels.jtokkit.Encodings
import com.knuddels.jtokkit.api.EncodingType

fun main() {
    val registry = Encodings.newDefaultEncodingRegistry()
    // O200K_BASE exists only in newer jtokkit versions; fall back to CL100K_BASE (verify)
    val enc = registry.getEncoding(EncodingType.O200K_BASE)

    val samples = linkedMapOf(
        "en" to "Where is the nearest train station?",
        "hi" to "निकटतम रेलवे स्टेशन कहाँ है?",
        "ja" to "最寄りの駅はどこですか？",
    )
    val base = enc.countTokens(samples.getValue("en"))
    for ((lang, text) in samples) {
        val n = enc.countTokens(text)
        val bytes = text.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8).size
        // prints: language, UTF-8 bytes, tokens, premium vs English
        println("$lang bytes=$bytes tokens=$n premium=${"%.2f".format(n.toDouble() / base)}x")
    }
}

Java with jtokkit.

import com.knuddels.jtokkit.Encodings;
import com.knuddels.jtokkit.api.Encoding;
import com.knuddels.jtokkit.api.EncodingRegistry;
import com.knuddels.jtokkit.api.EncodingType;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class TokenPremium {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EncodingRegistry registry = Encodings.newDefaultEncodingRegistry();
        Encoding enc = registry.getEncoding(EncodingType.O200K_BASE); // verify in jtokkit version
        Map<String, String> samples = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        samples.put("en", "Where is the nearest train station?");
        samples.put("hi", "निकटतम रेलवे स्टेशन कहाँ है?");
        samples.put("ja", "最寄りの駅はどこですか？");
        int base = enc.countTokens(samples.get("en"));
        samples.forEach((lang, text) -> {
            int n = enc.countTokens(text);
            int bytes = text.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).length;
            // prints: language, UTF-8 bytes, tokens, premium vs English
            System.out.printf("%s bytes=%d tokens=%d premium=%.2fx%n", lang, bytes, n, (double) n / base);
        });
    }
}

Important: this is an estimate for Claude. Claude, Gemini and Llama use their own tokenizers, so tiktoken counts are only a proxy. For exact Claude counts, use the provider's counting endpoint, which returns the token count without running the model.

Python, exact count for Claude (the Messages token-counting endpoint).

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
resp = client.messages.count_tokens(  # verify the method path in the SDK docs
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "निकटतम रेलवे स्टेशन कहाँ है?"}],
)
print(resp.input_tokens)  # prints the exact input token count

Kotlin and Java for exact Claude counts. The Anthropic Java SDK (com.anthropic:anthropic-java) exposes a token-counting call under the messages service; the exact class and method names change between versions, so verify in the SDK docs rather than copying a guessed signature. Kotlin uses the same Java SDK. Until verified, use the REST endpoint POST /v1/messages/count_tokens from OkHttp or Ktor, with the x-api-key and anthropic-version headers and a JSON body identical to a normal Messages request.

Real products. Many production gateways (LiteLLM, Helicone, internal proxies) count tokens before sending a request to enforce budgets and rate limits, and log tokens per language to catch cost drift.

Real life. It is weighing luggage on the airline's own scale. A bathroom scale at home (a different tokenizer) is close but not what you are charged by.

Tech. Token counting endpoints tokenize server-side with the exact production tokenizer and add the overhead of the chat template (role markers, system prompt formatting). That overhead is why the count for a message is a few tokens above the count of its raw text.

Common interview traps.

  • Using len(text) / 4 for non-English text, or a tiktoken count to bill a Claude workload.
  • Counting only the user text and forgetting system prompt, tool definitions, chat-template tokens and the previous conversation turns.
  • Measuring on three sample sentences. Build a per-language corpus from real traffic (hundreds of messages) and report mean and 95th percentile.

notes.title: Cost arithmetic with worked numbers
notes.html:
Setup (all prices are placeholders, not real quotes; verify current prices on the provider page). Assume input costs $3 per million tokens and output costs $15 per million tokens. Assume a support chatbot with a 500-token English prompt (system prompt plus question) and a 300-token English answer, 10,000 requests per day.

English baseline.

input  per request: 500 tokens
output per request: 300 tokens
daily input : 10,000 x 500 = 5,000,000 tokens  -> 5 x $3  = $15.00
daily output: 10,000 x 300 = 3,000,000 tokens  -> 3 x $15 = $45.00
daily total = $60.00;   30 days = $1,800

Same product in a language with a 2.5x premium (user text only). Careful: only text in that language inflates. The system prompt may still be English. Suppose the 500 input tokens are 200 (English system prompt) + 300 (user question) and the answer is generated in the user's language.

user question:  300 x 2.5 = 750 tokens
input  per request: 200 + 750 = 950 tokens
output per request: 300 x 2.5 = 750 tokens

daily input : 10,000 x 950 = 9.5M tokens  -> 9.5 x $3  = $28.50
daily output: 10,000 x 750 = 7.5M tokens  -> 7.5 x $15 = $112.50
daily total = $141.00;   30 days = $4,230
ratio vs English = 141 / 60 = 2.35x

The overall ratio (2.35x) is below the language premium (2.5x) because the English system prompt did not inflate. Notice that output is the larger lever: it is priced higher and it all inflates.

Embeddings and RAG add their own cost. Embedding models have their own tokenizers and limits (for example a maximum of 512 or 8,192 tokens per input). A chunk of 512 English tokens covers about 380 words; the same 512-token cap covers only about 100 to 150 words of Hindi. If you chunk by tokens, Hindi chunks hold less meaning and retrieval quality can fall. If you chunk by characters, Hindi chunks may exceed the model limit and be silently truncated. Measure chunk tokens per language.

Prompt caching helps the fixed part. A large system prompt reused across requests can be cached (provider feature; prices and minimum sizes vary, verify). Cached tokens are cheaper. Since the system prompt is usually English, caching is a strong lever for multilingual products: the unavoidable inflated part is the user text and the answer.

Batch and model tier. A smaller model (for example a Haiku-class model) at a fraction of the price can erase the premium; routing simple multilingual queries to a cheaper tier is often cheaper than trying to compress text.

Real products. Duolingo, Booking.com-style support bots and customer-service vendors that serve many countries report separate cost lines by market; global SaaS teams commonly keep one English system prompt and let the model answer in the user's language to avoid translating long instructions.

Real life. It is a taxi meter that ticks per block. A route through a district with many short blocks costs more for the same distance.

Tech. Cost = (input tokens x input price) + (output tokens x output price). A language premium multiplies only the portion of tokens in that language, and the output multiplier matters most because output is usually the priced-higher side.

Common interview traps.

  • Applying the premium to the whole prompt, including the English system prompt, and overstating the cost. Split by part.
  • Forgetting that the output language is chosen by the model and prompt. Asking "answer in English" for an internal agent can cut output cost.
  • Ignoring reasoning tokens: a reasoning model "thinks" in tokens too, and thinking in a high-premium language is more expensive than thinking in English.

notes.title: Latency and the context window
notes.html:
Latency. LLM generation is autoregressive: one token per forward pass, strictly in sequence. Total generation time is roughly:

time ~ time_to_first_token + (output tokens / tokens per second)

Example: decode speed = 50 tokens/s
  English answer, 300 tokens:           300 / 50 = 6.0 s
  Language with 2.5x premium, 750 tok:  750 / 50 = 15.0 s

The user feels this directly. Streaming (showing tokens as they arrive) hides part of it but a long answer in a high-premium language is simply slow. Time to first token also grows with input length: a bigger prompt means a longer prefill (the one-time pass over all input tokens), which scales roughly with input tokens, and attention cost grows faster than linearly in sequence length.

Context window. The window is measured in tokens, not words.

window = 200,000 tokens
English at ~1.3 tokens/word   -> ~153,000 words
Language at 4 tokens/word     -> ~50,000 words
Language at 6 tokens/word     -> ~33,000 words

So a "long-document" feature that works for an English contract can fail for the same contract in Hindi: the document plus instructions plus the output budget no longer fit. The output token limit (max_tokens) also bites sooner: a limit of 1,024 tokens ends an English answer at about 780 words but a high-premium answer at about 250 words, which can cut it off mid-sentence. Check stop_reason (it will say the output hit the maximum tokens) and raise the limit per language.

KV cache memory. During generation the model stores key/value vectors per token per layer (the KV cache; see the long-context notes). More tokens means more GPU memory per request, so self-hosted servers fit fewer concurrent high-premium requests. Capacity planning for a multilingual self-hosted service has to use tokens per request by language, not requests per second alone.

Real products. vLLM and TGI schedulers batch by tokens; their metrics (tokens per second, KV cache usage) show the effect of language mix directly. Chat UIs that stream (ChatGPT, Claude.ai, Gemini) hide part of the latency but cannot hide a very long output.

Real life. A conveyor belt where each item in a long sentence takes one tick. A language that needs more items per idea simply takes more ticks to deliver the same message.

Tech. Decode is memory-bandwidth bound: each new token requires reading the model weights and the KV cache, so latency per token is roughly constant, and total latency is linear in token count.

Common interview traps.

  • Setting one max_tokens for all locales; non-English answers get truncated.
  • Testing latency only in English and promising the same SLA for Hindi or Thai users.
  • Saying a larger context window removes the problem. It raises the ceiling but the premium still divides the usable content.

notes.title: Tokenizer families and vocabulary size
notes.html:
Why vocabulary size matters here. A bigger vocabulary can hold more multi-character pieces for more scripts, so fertility drops. But it costs memory: the embedding table and the output layer each have vocab x d_model parameters.

Math. With vocab 256,000 and d_model 4,096: 256,000 x 4,096 = 1,048,576,000, about 1.05 billion parameters in the embedding table, and about the same again in the output projection unless the two are tied. With vocab 32,000 and the same width: 131 million. So a bigger vocabulary can add over a billion parameters; for a 7B model that is a significant share, and for small models the cost is a large fraction of the total.

Common families (facts to verify before quoting).

Family Typical tokenizer Approx. vocab Multilingual note
OpenAI GPT-3.5 / 4 cl100k_base, byte-level BPE ~100k English-heavy, high premium for Indic and SEA scripts
OpenAI GPT-4o and later o200k_base, byte-level BPE ~200k Better compression for many non-English languages
Llama 2 SentencePiece BPE, byte fallback 32k Weak for non-Latin scripts
Llama 3 tiktoken-style BPE ~128k Improved, still English-leaning
Gemma SentencePiece ~256k Designed for multilingual use
mT5, XLM-R SentencePiece Unigram 250k Trained on balanced multilingual data
Claude, Gemini Proprietary not public Use the provider's counting endpoint

Switching tokenizers is not a drop-in. You cannot change a trained model's tokenizer without retraining or heavy adaptation. Teams adapting open models to a language (for example for Indic languages or Arabic) sometimes extend the vocabulary: add new tokens for the language, initialize their embeddings (often from the average of the old sub-token embeddings), and continue pretraining on that language. Examples include Indic and Arabic adaptations of Llama; check each project for details. This lowers fertility, but needs continued training, and the old and new tokens must be trained together to avoid damaging the original behavior.

Choosing a model for a multilingual product.

  1. Collect 200 to 500 real messages per target language.
  2. Count tokens per candidate model with its own tokenizer or counting endpoint.
  3. Multiply by the price per token for input and output, giving the effective cost per message.
  4. Compare quality on the same set (a small labeled eval), because a cheaper tokenizer on a weaker model is not a win.

Real products. Sarvam, AI4Bharat and others published Indic-focused tokenizers and models; Qwen models are tuned for Chinese plus English; Aya from Cohere targets many languages. Product names, sizes and token numbers change quickly (verify).

Real life. Choosing a suitcase size: a bigger suitcase carries more kinds of clothes but is heavy and costs more to check in.

Tech. It is a trade-off between sequence compression (shorter inputs) and parameter overhead (bigger embedding and softmax layers), plus the issue of rare tokens that get little training (under-trained or "glitch" tokens).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a new model version always lowers token counts. A new tokenizer can also increase counts for some content; re-measure on every model upgrade.
  • Forgetting that the vocabulary change shifts all your budget numbers, rate-limit assumptions and cache keys.
  • Thinking vocabulary extension is free: the new embeddings need training data in the target language.

notes.title: Quality, fairness and the hidden effects
notes.html:
Quality is not only cost. More tokens per idea means the model has to reason across more steps and the attention pattern is spread over a longer sequence. Several effects have been reported (verify for your model):

  • Accuracy on benchmarks tends to be lower in languages with high fertility, partly because those languages also had less training data, so the two causes are hard to separate.
  • Long fragments (single bytes or sub-syllable pieces) carry little meaning on their own, so the model builds meaning from many pieces and is more error-prone with rare words and names.
  • Few-shot examples consume more of the prompt budget, so you can fit fewer of them.

Fairness and access. Per-token pricing means the same answer costs more for speakers of high-premium languages, and context limits restrict how much they can submit. This is why "tokenizer parity" is discussed as a product fairness issue, not only a technical one. Free-tier quotas counted in tokens run out sooner for these users.

Prompt language choice. Many teams write the system prompt and tool descriptions in English (cheap, best-supported) and instruct the model to reply in the user's language. This is a common pattern, but check two things: output quality in that language and whether the model drifts back to English on long turns.

Translation pipelines. An alternative is translate-in, answer-in-English, translate-out. It reduces tokens in the main model call but adds latency, extra cost for the translation calls and translation errors (names, numbers, idioms). Usually only worth it for very high volume, or when the main model is weak in the language.

Normalization and mixed scripts. Code-mixed text ("Hinglish": Hindi in Latin letters) can tokenize more efficiently than Devanagari Hindi on English-heavy tokenizers, but with spelling variation that hurts retrieval. Normalizing Unicode (NFC/NFKC) before embedding and caching removes a class of duplicate and mismatch bugs.

Real products. Google Translate-style pipelines, WhatsApp-based assistants in India and Africa (often mixing languages and scripts), and Indic voice assistants all deal with code-mixing; some route by detected language to different models.

Real life. Imagine an exam in which a student must write each word using many tiny stickers instead of a single sheet. They can do it, but slowly, with more chance of a mistake, and with less room on the page.

Tech. Perplexity per token is not comparable across tokenizers. Compare models with bits per character or bits per byte, which normalize for tokenization differences.

Common interview traps.

  • Comparing perplexity numbers between models with different tokenizers. They are not on the same scale.
  • Assuming translating everything to English first is always cheaper end to end.
  • Ignoring that a quality gap and a cost gap compound: the worst-served language is both costlier and less accurate.

notes.title: Budgeting and mitigation playbook
notes.html:
Step 1: measure. Log input tokens, output tokens, language and model per request (most APIs return usage in the response). Compute mean and 95th percentile tokens per language weekly.

Step 2: set budgets per locale, not global. A single max_tokens and a single per-user quota is unfair and breaks. Use a language multiplier table built from your measurements.

Python, a simple per-language budget helper (shortcut: multipliers are static, refresh them after every model change).

# Premiums measured on YOUR traffic with YOUR model's tokenizer (example values).
PREMIUM = {"en": 1.0, "es": 1.4, "ru": 2.2, "hi": 3.5, "th": 4.0}

def output_limit(lang: str, english_tokens_needed: int, hard_cap: int = 4096) -> int:
    """max_tokens to request so a normal answer is not cut off in this language."""
    mult = PREMIUM.get(lang, 4.0)           # unknown language: assume the worst measured
    return min(hard_cap, int(english_tokens_needed * mult * 1.15))  # 15% safety margin

print(output_limit("en", 300))  # 345
print(output_limit("hi", 300))  # 1207   (300 * 3.5 * 1.15 = 1207.5, truncated to int)

Kotlin.

val premium = mapOf("en" to 1.0, "es" to 1.4, "ru" to 2.2, "hi" to 3.5, "th" to 4.0)

fun outputLimit(lang: String, englishTokens: Int, hardCap: Int = 4096): Int {
    val mult = premium[lang] ?: 4.0 // unknown language: assume the worst measured
    return minOf(hardCap, (englishTokens * mult * 1.15).toInt())
}

fun main() {
    println(outputLimit("en", 300)) // 345
    println(outputLimit("hi", 300)) // 1207
}

Java.

import java.util.Map;

public class Budget {
    static final Map<String, Double> PREMIUM =
        Map.of("en", 1.0, "es", 1.4, "ru", 2.2, "hi", 3.5, "th", 4.0);

    static int outputLimit(String lang, int englishTokens, int hardCap) {
        double mult = PREMIUM.getOrDefault(lang, 4.0); // unknown language: assume worst
        return Math.min(hardCap, (int) (englishTokens * mult * 1.15));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(outputLimit("en", 300, 4096)); // 345
        System.out.println(outputLimit("hi", 300, 4096)); // 1207
    }
}

Step 3: pull the levers, in rough order of payoff.

  1. Right-size the model. A cheaper model tier for simple multilingual intents.
  2. Cache the fixed prefix. English system prompt, tool schemas and few-shot examples cached with provider prompt caching.
  3. Shorten the output. Instruct "answer in at most N sentences", use structured output with short field names or codes instead of prose.
  4. Keep instructions in English and ask only for the answer in the user's language.
  5. Trim retrieved context. Fewer, better chunks; a reranker before the prompt; chunk by tokens measured in each language.
  6. Compress history. Summarize old turns; a high-premium language makes long chat history expensive quickly.
  7. Choose a better tokenizer. Evaluate models with balanced multilingual tokenizers; for self-hosted models consider a language-adapted variant.
  8. Set alerts. Cost per request by language, share of truncated answers by language.

On-device and Android. If you use on-device models (Gemini Nano via ML Kit GenAI, MediaPipe LLM Inference), the supported languages and token limits are fixed per model and device; verify the language list in the docs. The context window and memory budget on device is small, so a high-premium language gets very little usable context. Always call your own backend for cloud models and keep token accounting there, never in the app.

Real products. Gateways such as LiteLLM, Portkey and Helicone provide per-model cost tracking; provider dashboards show tokens by model. Teams commonly add a "language" tag to each request to break costs down.

Real life. A household budget with one line per family member: you cannot manage the grocery bill by looking at a single total, and each person's needs differ.

Tech. The budget is a function of three measured quantities per locale: tokens in, tokens out and price per token; every lever above reduces one of those.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing "compress the text" as the main fix; most savings come from model choice, caching and output length.
  • Applying one hard output cap for all languages, truncating answers in high-premium languages.
  • Optimizing the average while the 95th percentile (long documents in the worst language) triggers the outage or the bill.

notes.title: Production failure patterns
notes.html:
1. Truncated answers only in some languages. Symptom: support tickets from Thai or Hindi users saying answers stop mid-sentence; English users are fine. Cause: a single max_tokens. Diagnosis: the response stop_reason is the max-tokens value in a large share of non-English responses. Fix: per-language limits and an alert on truncation rate by locale.

2. Context overflow on long documents. Symptom: HTTP 400 "prompt is too long" or silent dropping of the oldest messages, only for some customers. Cause: window sized with English words per token. Fix: count tokens before sending (counting endpoint), return a clear error or chunk with map-reduce summarization.

3. Budget alarm after launching in a new market. Symptom: cost per active user triples after launching in India or Southeast Asia, though traffic is as forecast. Cause: forecast used English token counts. Fix: pilot with real text, forecast with measured premium, add a per-market budget.

4. Rate limits hit earlier than expected. Tokens-per-minute limits are counted in tokens; a high-premium user base reaches them with fewer requests. Fix: budget TPM per language mix and request a quota increase with measured numbers.

5. Embedding chunk truncation. Symptom: retrieval quality drops for non-English documents. Cause: chunk size in characters exceeds the embedding model's token limit and the tail is dropped silently. Fix: chunk by token count with the embedding model's tokenizer; log truncation.

6. Cache misses from Unicode forms. The same text in NFC and NFD produces different bytes, different tokens and a different hash, so prompt caches and response caches miss. Fix: normalize (NFC) before hashing and sending.

7. Billing mismatch with estimates. Finance compares the provider invoice to your tiktoken-based estimate and finds a gap. Cause: different tokenizer plus chat-template overhead. Fix: use the usage field returned by the API as the source of truth and use estimates only for pre-flight checks.

8. Mixed-language prompts doubling cost. The system prompt gets translated into 12 languages "for quality" and grows each time; a long English prompt would have worked and been cached. Fix: test English instructions against translated ones on an eval set before paying for the translation.

Real products. These patterns appear in public postmortems and community threads of teams building chat assistants for multiple markets; the details differ but the root cause is almost always English-only assumptions in token math.

Real life. A shop that prices shipping by the weight of English-sized boxes, then is surprised by the bill when the goods arrive in odd-shaped crates.

Tech. The common thread is that a single global constant (output limit, chunk size, context estimate, forecast) was derived from English and applied to all locales.

Common interview traps.

  • Diagnosing "model quality" when the real cause is truncation or context overflow.
  • Using estimates as billing truth instead of the API usage field.
  • Fixing one locale by tuning and forgetting to add an automated per-language regression test.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Tokens, not words or characters, are what you pay for, wait for and fit in the context window. Token count for the same meaning depends on language and script.
  • Fertility (tokens per word) or the parity premium (tokens vs English on parallel text) is the metric. Latin-script European languages are often 1.2 to 2x English, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic and Hebrew 2 to 3x, and Indic and Southeast Asian scripts up to 4 to 10x on older tokenizers (illustrative; always re-measure).
  • The mechanism: byte-level BPE trained on English-heavy data; UTF-8 uses 1 byte for ASCII, 2 for Cyrillic/Arabic/Hebrew, 3 for Indic/Thai/CJK, 4 for emoji; scripts without merges approach one token per byte, and byte fallback costs 2 to 4 tokens per rare character.
  • Cost, latency and context all scale with the premium. Output tokens usually dominate: they cost more per token and are generated one at a time. Only the part of the prompt that is in the high-premium language inflates, so keep the system prompt in English and cache it.
  • Larger vocabularies (200k to 256k) and balanced training data lower fertility, at the cost of a bigger embedding and output layer. A new model version can change your numbers either way.
  • Measure with the model's own tokenizer or counting endpoint, on real per-language data; use the API usage field as billing truth.
  • Budget per locale: per-language max_tokens, per-market cost forecast, truncation alerts, token-based chunking for RAG, Unicode normalization.
  • Quality and fairness matter too: high-fertility languages tend to be both costlier and less accurate; compare models with bits per byte, not raw perplexity.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting one number ("non-English is 2x") instead of explaining it varies by language, script and tokenizer, and must be measured.
  • Mixing up characters, code points, bytes and tokens.
  • Stopping at "use a cheaper model" without separating the cost levers: premium, output length, caching, tier, and truncation risk.
